title: The art of storytelling
goals: Front places, participles and adjectives with inversion (In the doorway stood a man; Hidden beneath the floor lay…) to control where the reader's eye lands.
Use literary emphatic fronting: Gone are the days…, Such was the…, So quiet was…, Not a word did he say.
Omit what is recoverable (ellipsis after auxiliaries, to and in coordination) to build rhythm without losing clarity.
Substitute with so, not, do so, one/ones and the former/the latter, and know when they sound natural or overly formal.
Choose verbs of movement, looking and speech with precision, and atmospheric adjectives with narrative weight.
Narrate an anecdote with style (narrative markers, rhythm, suspense) and rewrite a flat text to improve it.

learn.title: Fronting of place and of participles with inversion
learn.html:
In narrative, a place adverbial or a participle is placed at the beginning to "move the camera": first the scene, and at the end the important thing. When the verb expresses position, movement or existence, the subject and the verb are inverted (without do).

DeviceStandard orderWith fronting
Place + verb of positionA man stood in the doorway.In the doorway stood a man.
Place + movementA cart rolled down the hill.Down the hill rolled a cart.
Past participle / adjective + beA bundle of letters was hidden beneath the floorboards.Hidden beneath the floorboards was a bundle of letters.
Present participleA lone cyclist was standing in the rain.Standing in the rain was a lone cyclist.
here / there / now / thenThe bus comes here.Here comes the bus. (but with a pronoun: Here it comes!)
  • Only with intransitive verbs of position, movement or appearance (stand, lie, sit, hang, come, go, walk, rise, appear, follow, be). It does not work with transitive verbs.
  • With a subject pronoun there is NO inversion: In the corner she sat, not In the corner sat she.
  • Do not add do: inversion after a fronted place uses the lexical verb (Into the room walked a stranger), which is different from the auxiliary inversion in the next block.
  • End of sentence = focus: the new and important element (the subject) is left at the end, where the reader receives it with the most weight.
  • Register: literary and journalistic; in conversation it sounds theatrical, except Here we go, There goes… and Here comes….

watch.wrong: On the top shelf sat she, quietly reading.
watch.right: On the top shelf she sat, quietly reading.
watch.why: With a subject pronoun there is no inversion.

watch.wrong: Into the room did walk a stranger.
watch.right: Into the room walked a stranger.
watch.why: Fronted place inverts the lexical verb, with no do.

watch.wrong: Sat on the bench an old man.
watch.right: On the bench sat an old man.
watch.why: What is fronted is the place adverbial, not the verb alone.

watch.wrong: Hidden under the bed found she the letter.
watch.right: Hidden under the bed was the letter.
watch.why: With a transitive verb it is not fronted this way; use be + past participle, with the subject at the end.

learn.title: Emphatic fronting: Gone are the days…, Such was…, So…was…
learn.html:
Besides place, the complement or the adjective can be fronted to give solemnity, emphasis or cadence. It almost always requires subject-verb inversion.

PatternExampleNote
Gone / Long gone are the days when…Gone are the days when children played in the street until dark.Nostalgia or the end of an era. It agrees with the noun: Gone is the era…
Such was + noun + that…Such was the force of the blast that every window shattered.= so great was… that.
So + adjective + was/were + subject + that…So quiet was the street that every footstep echoed.Adjective + be + subject + that.
Not a / Not one / Not once + auxiliary + subjectNot a word did she say all evening.Fronted negative: auxiliary before the subject.
Only then / Only after / Only when + auxiliary + subjectOnly then did he realise what she meant.Restrictive: inversion in the main clause.
Hardly / No sooner had… when / thanHardly had we left when it began to rain.C1 review: inversion with negative adverbs.
Adjective of evaluation + beFortunate are those who never have to choose.Proverbial or oratorical tone.
  • Mind the order: So terrible was the storm that… (adjective, verb, subject), not So terrible the storm was that….
  • Such was the + abstract noun (force, shock, silence); you do not say Such a beautiful was….
  • Do not overuse these: two or three fronted structures in a text add style; six in one paragraph sound like pastiche.

watch.wrong: So terrible the storm was that the ferry never left.
watch.right: So terrible was the storm that the ferry never left.
watch.why: After So + a fronted adjective, the verb and the subject are inverted.

watch.wrong: Gone the days are when he could just walk out.
watch.right: Gone are the days when he could just walk out.
watch.why: Gone + are + subject: inverts the verb.

watch.wrong: Not a word she said all evening.
watch.right: Not a word did she say all evening.
watch.why: A fronted negative complement requires an auxiliary before the subject.

learn.title: Ellipsis: saying less to say more
learn.html:
Ellipsis omits what the listener can already recover. It is not carelessness: it gives rhythm, avoids heaviness and, in narrative, leaves gaps for the reader to fill.

ContextWith repetitionWith ellipsis
Subject in coordinationTom opened the drawer and Tom took out a letter.Tom opened the drawer and took out a letter.
After an auxiliaryShe has finished her report, but I haven't finished yet.She has finished her report, but I haven't yet.
After toHe asked me to join, but I didn't want to join.He asked me to join, but I didn't want to.
Gapping (repeated verb)Some guests arrived early, others arrived late.Some guests arrived early, others late.
Answers— Will you come? — I will come.— Will you come? — I will. / I'd love to.
Indirect questions (sluicing)He's leaving, but I don't know why he's leaving.He's leaving, but I don't know why.
Telegraphic / diary styleI went out. I saw nothing.Went out. Saw nothing.
  • Golden rule: you can omit whatever is identical and recoverable; the auxiliary (or to) stays as an "anchor".
  • Right auxiliary: if the original sentence had no auxiliary, use do/does/did (I like it, and so does she); do not invent auxiliaries that are not there.
  • Narrative: She wanted to say something. She didn't. The omitted verb carries more weight than a written one.
  • Not valid if it creates ambiguity. If the reader is unsure what was omitted, repeat it.

watch.wrong: She said she'd call, but she didn't to.
watch.right: She said she'd call, but she didn't.
watch.why: After an auxiliary the verb is omitted; to appears only when it replaces an infinitive (I didn't want to).

watch.wrong: I'd love to come, but I can't to.
watch.right: I'd love to come, but I can't.
watch.why: Can is a modal: it is not followed by to.

watch.wrong: I've never been to Oaxaca, but my sister has been it.
watch.right: I've never been to Oaxaca, but my sister has.
watch.why: Everything that can be recovered after the auxiliary is elided (e.g. 'has been to Oaxaca').

learn.title: Substitution: so, not, do so, one/ones, the former/the latter
learn.html:
Substitution replaces a fragment with a "stand-in" word. It maintains cohesion and avoids heavy repetition.

DeviceUseExample
so / not after verbs of opinionI think / hope / suppose / believe / expect / suspect / guess / am afraid so. Negative: I hope / suspect / am afraid not; with think and believe: I don't think so or I think not (more formal).— Is she coming? — I'm afraid so.
if so / if notThey replace a whole clause.If so, we'll leave; if not, we'll wait.
do soReplaces a verb + complement; more formal than do it.She told him to leave and he did so without a word.
one / onesReplace a countable noun; they work with adjectives and with this/that/which/the.I lost my umbrella, so I bought a new one. These boots are tight; have you got bigger ones?
the former / the latterThe first / the second of two elements mentioned.Of tea and coffee, I prefer the latter.
so do I / neither do IAgreement with inversion.— I love it. — So do I.
the same / likewiseReplace an action or quality already mentioned.He apologised, and she did the same.
  • One/ones do not replace uncountable nouns (I prefer the red wine, not the red one if you are talking about wine in general), nor do they follow a possessive without an adjective (my one is wrong; mine is right).
  • With a bare comparative adjective, English requires the substitute: bigger ones, not bigger.
  • So/not never take it: I hope so, not I hope it.

watch.wrong: — Is she coming? — I hope it.
watch.right: — Is she coming? — I hope so.
watch.why: After hope, suppose, think…, the short answer uses so / not, not it.

watch.wrong: These shoes are too tight; do you have bigger?
watch.right: These shoes are too tight; do you have bigger ones?
watch.why: With a comparative adjective and no noun, you must use ones.
Possessive pronouns already replace the noun; one is redundant.

learn.title: Narrative markers and rhythm control
learn.html:
• Long story short / To cut a long story short — to make a long story short: jumps to the outcome.
  • Fast-forward to… — skipping ahead to…: jumps in time.
  • Little did I know… — "what I did not know…": creates suspense (inversion with a negative adverb).
  • Out of nowhere / Out of the blue — suddenly, without warning.
  • The next thing I knew… — and then, suddenly…: speeds things up.
  • As luck would have it — as chance would have it (good or bad).
  • There I was, -ing… — "there I was…": the scene of an oral anecdote.
  • Come to think of it / Mind you — on reflection / mind you, though: adds a nuance or a twist.
  • In the nick of time — just in time.
  • To make matters worse — to top it all.
  • dine out on a story — to live off telling an anecdote (boasting about it at dinner parties).

Rhythm: alternate long sentences that build up with short sentences that cut sharply; keep the most important element for the end of the sentence; use fronting to set the scene and ellipsis to speed things up. Read aloud: if you breathe where you should not, rewrite.

write.prompt: Write the opening of a story of 300 to 400 words (third person, past tense) that begins in medias res. Use at least three fronted structures (one with place and inversion, one with Such/So… was, one with Not/Only…), three ellipses and two substitutions (so, one, did so). Include five verbs or adjectives from the unit (squint, slink, murmur, ominous, dilapidated…). Alternate long and short sentences.
checklist: 300–400 words, past-tense narrative with an opening hook
One fronted place with correct inversion (In the doorway stood…, with no inverted pronoun)
A Such was… or So + adjective + was + subject + that… structure
A negative fronting (Not a word did…; Only then did…)
Three ellipses (shared subject, auxiliary, to) without ambiguity
At least one substitution with so / one / did so
Five well-used words from the unit's vocabulary
Varied rhythm: at least one very short sentence that breaks the rhythm
write.model:
The first shot shattered the window above her head, and Mara ran.

She did not stop to look back. Down the alley she pelted, past the bins and the bicycles chained to rusting railings, until the street opened into a courtyard she had never seen. Ahead of her loomed a dilapidated warehouse, its roof sagging, its windows black. She slipped inside.

Dark. Silence. Somewhere above her, a pipe dripped.

In the far corner stood a man in a long grey coat, perfectly still. Mara squinted through the gloom and recognised him at once, and wished she had not. He was Aldous Crane, her father's old partner, and he had been dead for six years. Or so the newspapers had said.

"You're late," he murmured. He sounded neither angry nor surprised.

Such was her shock that she could not answer. Her mind, usually quick, had simply emptied itself. Not a word did she manage to say; she merely stared, one hand gripping the doorframe, the other clutching the satchel she had stolen that morning. Outside, footsteps crunched on gravel, slowly, deliberately, with an ominous patience that suggested their owner was in no hurry at all.

"They followed you," said Crane. "I told you they would."

"You told me nothing."

"Didn't I? Then I meant to." He smiled thinly. "Give me the satchel."

She hesitated. Only then did it occur to her that she had no idea whose side he was on, and perhaps never had. Her father had trusted him; her father was dead, too. If Crane wanted the satchel, it was because it held something worth killing for, and she thought she knew what. She had suspected so since dawn.

The door creaked. Crane raised one finger to his lips and began to slink backwards into the shadows, beckoning her to do the same. She did so, heart hammering.

A torch beam swept the floor. It paused. Then it swung, very slowly, towards her.

write.prompt: Rewrite the following flat passage as a text of 300 to 400 words that develops it and improves its rhythm and effect. Passage: «It was a hot afternoon. A woman came into the café. She sat at a table. She looked at the menu. A waiter came. She said she wanted a coffee. He brought it. She drank it. Then she left. She left a letter on the table.» Keep the facts, but add atmosphere, fronting, ellipsis, substitutions and a suspenseful closing. At the end, in two or three sentences in English, explain what changes you made and why.
checklist: 300–400 words, including the final 2–3 comment sentences
The passage's facts are kept (café, table, menu, waiter, coffee, departure, letter)
At least two fronted structures with correct inversion
Ellipsis and substitution to avoid repetition
At least three atmospheric adjectives or verbs with nuance (stagger, glimpse, eerie…)
One narrative marker (Little did she know, out of nowhere, the next thing…)
Variation in sentence length and a closing that leaves the letter in suspense
The final commentary clearly explains the style decisions
write.model:
That afternoon the heat pressed down on the city like a heavy hand. Inside the café, the ceiling fans turned lazily, stirring nothing but dust, and an eerie quiet hung over the empty tables.

Into this drowsy stillness walked a woman in a long coat, far too thick for the weather. Not once did she glance at the other customers. She chose a table by the window, sat down with her back to the wall and picked up the menu, though her eyes never seemed to read it. Her fingers trembled; the card rattled faintly against the glass.

A waiter appeared, young, bored and polishing a glass he had clearly polished already. She murmured that she would like a coffee, black, and he nodded, promising to bring one at once. Neither spoke further. Out on the street, a tram clanged and was gone.

The coffee arrived, dark and steaming, and she drank it slowly, as though each mouthful might be her last. Only when the cup was empty did she move. Rising abruptly, she dropped a few coins beside the saucer and, with a last glimpse over her shoulder at the door, slipped out into the glare.

Little did the waiter know what lay beneath the saucer. A letter, sealed and unstamped, with a single word written on the envelope. He lifted it, frowned and turned it over. It was addressed to him.

Commentary: I opened with an image of heat to build atmosphere, and I used fronted structures such as "Into this drowsy stillness walked a woman" and "Not once did she glance" to vary the rhythm. I replaced repeated subjects with ellipsis and substitutions ("bring one", "Neither spoke further"), and I kept sentences short in the tense moments. Finally, I moved the letter to the end so that the passage closes in suspense.

reading.title: The Fire Was Never the Point
reading.intro: Read this essay on the art of storytelling and answer the questions. Notice how the text itself uses the structures it describes.
paragraphs: Gone are the days when stories were told around a fire, and with them, we are told, has gone the art. I am not convinced. What has changed is the audience, not the craft; and the craft, I have come to believe, rests on a handful of unglamorous decisions that any teller, whether novelist, barrister or uncle at a wedding, makes in every sentence, consciously or otherwise.

The first is where to stand. Consider two openings. "It was a cold night, and a man was standing in the doorway." And: "In the doorway stood a man." The facts are identical; the effect is not. The first leaves you outside, listening to a report. The second puts you in the room, your eye sweeping from the scene to the figure, and it delays the one thing you most want to know until the very end of the sentence. That is what fronting does: it rearranges the order in which the reader meets the world. Nobody would call it complicated. Few writers, though, use it often enough, or sparingly enough.

The second decision is what to leave out. A good storyteller trusts the reader to fill the gaps. "She wanted to say something. She didn't." The second sentence is only two words long, and the missing verb does more work than the verb itself would have done. Ellipsis is not laziness; it is rhythm. The sentence that stops early makes us lean in. Writers of detective fiction have known this for a century: the clue is never explained, merely left lying there, like a glove on a stair.

Compare the old man who tells the same wedding anecdote at every family gathering. He leaves nothing out. "And then I opened the door, and I looked inside, and I saw that the room was empty, and I thought that someone had taken the paintings, and I was very upset." There is nothing wrong with the story. Everything is wrong with the telling. Every "and I" is a small tax on our patience. Cut it to "I opened the door. The room was empty. The paintings were gone," and the same material acquires the sound of an event.

Substitution does a related job. A story that says "the red car" four times in one paragraph starts to sound like an instruction manual; one that says "the red one", or lets "it" do the work, keeps the camera moving. Likewise the humble "so". "Would she come back? Nobody thought so." The two-word reply closes the question without ceremony and carries, in its flatness, a verdict.

Then there is the matter of vocabulary, and here a warning is in order. It is tempting to believe that richer words make richer stories. Often they do the opposite. "He walked slowly" is not improved by "he sauntered" unless the sauntering is the point; the verb must earn its place. But when it does, when a woman "slinks" out of a party, a man "peers" at a letter he would rather not read, a house is "dilapidated" rather than merely old, the reader sees something no adjective-and-adverb combination could supply. The word is doing a small piece of characterisation. It is also doing it quietly, which is the only way characterisation survives.

Such is the paradox of style: the best sentences feel inevitable, and yet they are the product of dozens of small choices that might have gone the other way. Never have I written a paragraph that I could not improve by reading it aloud. Only then does one hear the pulse, the long sentence that gathers speed and the short one that stops it dead. Rhythm is, in the end, a form of honesty about how events feel: sometimes they drift, and sometimes they hit.

So, to the writer who fears the fire has gone out, I would say only this. The fire was never the point. Somebody sat near it and decided what to say first, what to hold back, and when to stop. Those decisions are still ours to make, and no software has yet made them for us, at least not with any conviction. Nobody has yet persuaded a room to fall silent with an average.

listening.title: The best man
listening.intro: Listen to Sam telling an anecdote to his friends. He speaks fast, uses idioms and follows the rhythm of a real conversation. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Go on then, Sam, tell Nadia about the wedding. I've heard it twice and I'm still not sure I believe it.
Right, so, picture the scene. Ten minutes before the ceremony, and there I am in the car park, suit on, no ring.
The groom's, obviously. I was the best man. I'd put it in my jacket pocket, and the jacket was, as luck would have it, still hanging in my flat, forty minutes away.
You're joking. What did you do?
Well, I did what any sensible person would do. I panicked. Out of nowhere, this little old lady comes up and says, "Are you all right, love?" and I blurted out the whole thing.
And this is where it gets ridiculous.
Hang on, let me tell it. Long story short, she took off her own wedding ring, fifty years she'd worn it, mind you, and said, "Borrow mine. Just don't lose it."
Did I what? Lose it? Not a chance. Not a word did I say all through the ceremony. I held that ring like a live grenade.
Only afterwards did he realise the old lady was the groom's grandmother.
Which, to be fair, I didn't know. Little did I know she'd been sizing me up the whole time.
I'd like to think so. Anyway, she gave me a wink at the reception, and, well, I've been dining out on it ever since.

tasks.prompt: Tell a real or invented anecdote (a mix-up, a trip, a stroke of luck) using narrative markers and at least one fronted structure.
questions: What's the funniest or strangest thing that has ever happened to you while travelling?
tasks.model: Picture the scene: it's midnight, I'm on a platform in a town I've never heard of, and the last train has gone. Out of nowhere, a man comes up and says, "You'll want the bus." Long story short, I ended up sharing a taxi with a retired brass band. Not a word of English did the driver speak, yet we sang the whole way. Little did I know I'd be invited to the concert the following night.
checklist: A clear opening scene (Picture the scene…)
A jump marker (Long story short / Fast-forward to…)
A fronted structure with inversion (Not a word… did…)
A closing with suspense or a twist (Little did I know…)

tasks.prompt: Describe a place with atmosphere (an old house, an empty station, a market) using unit adjectives and place fronting.
questions: What is a place you remember vividly?
What did it look and sound like?
How did it make you feel?
tasks.model: I remember a dilapidated cinema in my hometown. Above the entrance hung a broken neon sign, and inside, the cavernous hall smelled of dust. Stifling heat in summer; a hushed, almost eerie silence in winter. A sense of foreboding came over me whenever I walked down the aisle, yet I loved it. So quiet was the place that you could hear the projector breathe.
checklist: Two atmospheric adjectives (dilapidated, hushed, eerie…)
A place fronting with inversion (Above the entrance hung…)
A So + adj + was… structure
A personal feeling at the end

tasks.prompt: In two minutes, explain what makes a story good, and then retell it more briefly using ellipsis and substitution.
questions: Can you retell one in four sentences?
tasks.model: A good story knows what to leave out. Take the one about my uncle's lost dog. He looked everywhere. Found nothing. Then, two weeks later, the dog turned up at the door, thinner but unrepentant. I'd cut the long search; the search is the bit nobody remembers. Would you tell it that way? I would, and I'm sure most good storytellers do too.
checklist: Ellipsis of subject or auxiliary (Found nothing; I would)
A substitution (one, so, did so)
An opinion on what to cut
Rhythm: short sentences after a long one
